text: What would a pressure gauge above the liquid read as it warms and what must the molecules at the surface be doing to cause that?

I am studying why the vapor pressure of a liquid rises so steeply with temperature. Explain what the molecules at the surface are doing, using a liquid I have not named. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait for my answer.
In your own words what did the notebook show you about the molecules at the surface?
The problem is on your screen. Open the Equations list and pick the relation that expresses what you just described.
Which quantities in this problem were measured and which one is being inferred?

I need to recognise which equation links vapor pressure, temperature and heat of vaporization, in its two-point form and its straight-line form. Explain what each symbol stands for and when each form is the handy one. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait.
What does each symbol in the relation you need stand for?
The relation is ln(P2/P1) = -(ΔHvap/R)(1/T2 - 1/T1); the straight-line form is ln P = -(ΔHvap/R)(1/T) + C.
Before any numbers go in: rearrange your relation so the quantity you are after stands alone on the left. Type it out.
Which quantity is the one you are after and what is the last operation standing between it and being alone?

Show me how to rearrange an equation that has a natural log on one side and a difference of reciprocal temperatures on the other so that a chosen variable stands alone. Use symbols different from mine and do not use my numbers. Then give me one short practice rearrangement and wait for my answer.
What operation undoes a natural log and what undoes a reciprocal?
What must be true of a temperature before it can go into this relation? Convert and type the kelvin value(s).
What would it mean for the molecules if a temperature of zero on your scale were put into 1/T?
Explain why gas-law and vapor-pressure equations need absolute temperature, using an example I have not named. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait.
Why does this relation need an absolute temperature?
Add 273.15 to each Celsius temperature to get kelvin.
Look at the units of R and of the heat of vaporization. What has to happen before they meet in one fraction? Convert one of them and type the value with its unit.
What units must ΔHvap/R end up with for the equation to balance?
Explain how to keep energy units consistent between the gas constant R and a heat of vaporization given in kJ/mol. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait.
What did you find about the units of R and ΔHvap?
Either multiply ΔHvap in kJ/mol by 1000 to get J/mol or use R = 0.008314 kJ/(mol K).
The two pressures sit in one ratio. What must be true of their units? Convert one and type it.
What should the units of P2/P1 be?
Explain why two pressures in a ratio must share a unit and how atm, torr and kPa relate. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait.
What must be true of two pressures before you divide one by the other?
1 atm = 760 torr = 101.325 kPa. Put both pressures in the same unit.
Put your measured values into the relation and show me what you get for each side.
Which of your numbers came from an instrument and which are you about to infer?
Show me how to substitute values into the two-point vapor pressure relation and isolate an unknown, using numbers and a liquid different from mine. Then ask me one short question and wait.
What is the first thing you will do with your numbers now?
Substitute the kelvin temperatures and the matched pressures and keep ΔHvap and R in matching units. Then isolate the unknown.
Carry it through. What value do you get and in what units?
Before you calculate should the answer be larger or smaller than the value you were given and why?

Explain how to isolate an unknown from an equation with a natural log on one side and reciprocal temperatures on the other, using an example different from mine. Then ask me one short question and wait.
Which step of the algebra was blocking you?
Isolate the unknown: exponentiate both sides for a pressure; solve for 1/T and take the reciprocal for a temperature.
Before any numbers: write ΔHvap in terms of the slope of your line. Type the equation with ΔHvap alone on the left.
Set your straight line beside the relation you picked. Which group of symbols sits where the slope sits?

Show me how to rearrange a straight-line equation of the form ln(y) = m(1/x) + b for a chosen variable, and how a slope can stand for a physical quantity. Use symbols different from mine and no numbers of mine. Then give me one short practice rearrangement and wait for my answer.
Which part of the relation plays the part of the slope?
What does the slope of your line stand for and what heat of vaporization does it give? Type the value with its unit.
If the line were steeper what would that say about how hard it is for a molecule to leave the liquid?
Explain how the slope of a plot of ln P against 1/T gives the heat of vaporization, using data different from mine. Do not solve my problem. Then ask me one short question and wait.
How does the slope connect to the heat of vaporization?
Slope = -ΔHvap/R so ΔHvap = -(slope)(R).
Now rearrange your line so that T stands alone on the left. Type it.
What would the gauge read at the normal boiling point and where does that reading go in your line?

What undoes a reciprocal and in what order do you clear the terms around 1/T?
What defines the normal boiling point and where is that on your line? Type the temperature with its unit.
What would a pressure gauge read above the liquid at the moment it boils in an open beaker at sea level?

Explain what the normal boiling point means in terms of vapor pressure and how to find it from a straight-line fit of ln P against 1/T, using data different from mine. Then ask me one short question and wait.
What condition defines the normal boiling point?
Set P to 760 torr in your line and solve for T.
Look back at your result. What does it let you claim about molecules you never saw and how sure can you be?
What did the instrument actually measure and what did you infer from it?
